abstract: Evolutionary rescue can prevent population extinction following abrupt environmental change, but the genetic architectures that enable rapid adaptation under simultaneous strong selection and severe demographic bottlenecks remain poorly resolved. In particular, rescue may rely on either dispersed adaptive variants or clusters of tightly linked alleles that can respond to selection despite strong drift. We investigated the genetic architecture of evolutionary rescue in Callosobruchus maculatus, the cowpea seed beetle, following a shift to lentil, a novel and stressful host. To do so, we combined experimental evolution, whole-genome sequencing, backcross introgression, early-generation genomic sampling, association mapping, and transcriptomics. Initial adaptation produced widespread genomic differentiation, but backcrossing localized evidence for adaptive variation primarily to large regions on chromosomes 1 and 9. These regions contained large haploblocks with patterns consistent with suppressed recombination, possibly due to structural variation. On chromosome 9, a rare haplotype increased from approximately 0.5% to 48% in a single generation in one genetic background, consistent with extremely strong selection (s {approx} 0.9995). On chromosome 1, a 14 Mb haploblock contained nearly all genetic variation for two fitness-related traits and was associated with differential gene expression. Across genetic backgrounds, chromosome 1 was repeatedly implicated in adaptation, whereas lines from one source population additionally involved chromosome 9. Together, these results show that evolutionary rescue can rely on large, non-recombining haploblocks, providing a mechanism by which clustered genetic architectures can respond rapidly and repeatably despite severe population bottlenecks.
